summary: Ghost Rovers is an interactive web story for ages 6 to 10 about the NASA machines left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. Visitors pick a world showing the Moon, Mars, or Deep Space and tap a glowing marker on a real NASA map, and each machine tells its own story in its own voice: Apollo 15's science station, the rovers Spirit and Opportunity, the helicopter Ingenuity, the lander Insight, and the orbiters Dawn and NEAR Shoemaker. Each story explains what the machine was sent to do, how it worked, what it discovered, and where it rests now, with key facts and links to the NASA pages they come from. A Listen button tells the story.It addresses the challenge by turning forgotten hardware into characters children can connect with, showing how engineering and science fit together instead of listing dry facts. It matters because these machines' discoveries like ancient water on Mars, the trembling of another planet's interior, the first flight on another world and still shape exploration today, and the next generation should meet the explorers who made them, even though they never came home.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Ghost Rovers is an interactive web story that teaches school-age space fans about the NASA machines left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. A visitor picks a world, then taps a glowing signal on a real NASA map. The machine wakes up and tells its own story in the first person: why it was sent, how its hardware worked, what it found and how its mission ended. Seven machines are included: the Apollo 15 science station, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity, InSight, Dawn and NEAR Shoemaker. A Listen button plays narration, and the full text stays on screen. Every story ends with the machine’s NASA sources.

What benefits does it have?

Children usually hear only about active missions. Ghost Rovers gives these machines a voice, so facts about engineering and science stick as part of a story, not a list. It works on phones, laptops and tablets with no install. Parents and teachers can check every fact through the NASA links. It is free, and anyone can add a new machine by adding one entry to a data file.

What is the intended impact?

We want children to feel a personal connection to these robotic explorers and to see how the engineering of each machine led to what humanity learned. For example, Ingenuity’s big, fast blades made flight possible in thin air, and NEAR Shoemaker landed on an asteroid even though it was never built to. We hope this makes young people curious about space and science, and shows teachers an easy way to bring NASA history into class.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with all stories stored in one JSON file. No frameworks.
  • Data and images: NASA mission pages for facts and sources, and NASA images: the LRO Moon mosaic, the Viking Mars mosaic, and photos of Ceres (Dawn) and Eros (NEAR Shoemaker). The solar system map is drawn in SVG.
  • Narration: AI voices made with ElevenLabs, one MP3 per story. If a file is missing, the browser’s built-in voice is used.
  • Fonts: Fraunces and Atkinson Hyperlegible from Google Fonts.
  • Development: Git and GitHub Pages for hosting, a local Python web server and a headless browser for testing.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. It runs in any modern browser.

How is your project creative?

The machines tell their own stories. Each one speaks in its own imagined voice, with a hook, an ending and a “where I am now” line, so a technical mission becomes a character. Maps are real NASA images, and each machine appears as a glowing “ghost signal” you tap to wake up. Hard words, such as asteroid, geologist and magnetometer, are explained inside the story in kid-friendly language. Each ending matters emotionally: a dust storm, a cold night, a last flight, a call that is never answered.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Audience: we wrote for ages 6 to 10 in short sentences, so older readers can follow too.
  • Accuracy: facts were checked against NASA pages. We removed or reworded claims that were too strong, for example describing Apollo 15’s rover as the first rover driven by astronauts, not the first rover on the Moon. Where NASA pages gave different end dates, we linked the end-of-mission pages.
  • Accessibility: text always shown with audio, keyboard navigation, screen reader labels, light and dark modes, reduced motion, and large machine buttons on phones.
  • Focus: seven specific machines on three maps, not a long list.
  • Performance: audio loads only when a story is played, and the site is static, so it loads quickly.
